channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: Raleigh woman says company’s AI agent confused her over rent. Now she’s evicted.
item.description: WRAL: “A leasing office told a Raleigh woman she could pay her rent at the end of November, but when she received an eviction notice on Monday and called the leasing office, the leasing agent blamed it on a mistake by the company’s AI agent and said the woman would be evicted on Thursday.”

item.title: Data Centers Flood Black Communities Without Residents Having a Say
item.description: Capital B News: “Majority-Black communities are more than two times more likely to host a data center than majority-white ones and far less likely to receive the chance to hear about the projects before they’re approved or offer their opinion through public comment.”

item.title: NYISO warns of coming statewide power shortfall, with upstate data centers a key factor
item.description: Spectrum Local News: “New York’s power grid operator is warning the state could run short of electricity within the next decade, and much of the new demand driving the gap is expected to land in upstate New York.”

item.title: Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers
item.description: Ars Technica: “Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers.”

item.title: Iowa geologist: Groundwater monitoring needed if more data centers are coming
item.description: Iowa Capital Dispatch: “Data centers in Iowa currently have not had a huge impact on the state’s groundwater, but Iowa’s state geologist said Wednesday a more comprehensive groundwater monitoring network will be necessary if the state plans to have sustainable groundwater management while continuing to attract data centers and large users.”

item.title: Spotify is giving every artist a bouncer to keep AI slop off their page
item.description: DigitalTrends: “Spotify has opened Artist Profile Protection to all artists on the service, eight months after the initial test with a few thousand artists. It allows artists to review, and in some cases approve, music that’s being delivered under their name in Spotify for Artists.”

item.title: China attackers deployed AI agents that autonomously found and exploited a 0-day to take over a university server
item.description: The Register: “Suspected Chinese spies deployed AI agents which worked autonomously to find a zero-day in an open source application and then abuse the flaw to break into university networks, gaining full control of a server, according to Amazon CISO CJ Moses.”

item.title: Some US House Dems urge a national moratorium on buildup of new data centers
item.description: Missouri Independent: “Leading and incoming U.S. House Democrats called for a national moratorium on the development of new artificial intelligence data centers Tuesday.”

item.title: UC gives students free access to ChatGPT. Faculty say OpenAI deal is ‘unwise’
item.description: EdSource: “The University of California is procuring full access to ChatGPT Edu for all students and faculty as part of a $1.2 million agreement with OpenAI, despite concerns from faculty leaders about the academic consequences associated with artificial intelligence.”

item.title: Syracuse University to Use AI for Faster, More Consistent Reviews of Applications
item.description: Syracuse University: “Syracuse University today announced that its Office of Admissions will use artificial intelligence (AI) to support the review of undergraduate applications, beginning with this admissions cycle. Members of the admissions team will continue to read, evaluate and make decisions for each application; AI will never make admission decisions.”

item.title: Dartmouth to Pilot New Approaches to AI in Education
item.description: Dartmouth College: “A new slate of grants, computing investments, curricular initiatives, and campus programming will support both innovation and critical inquiry alongside efforts to develop ethical guidelines for the use of AI across schools.”

item.title: Many Etsy Sellers Close Up Shop Over Site’s New A.I. Policy
item.description: New York Times: “Many longtime owners of shops on Etsy, the online marketplace known for its handmade goods, said this week that they had left the site over a recently announced policy change that they said would leave them vulnerable to exploitation by artificial intelligence companies. Language in Etsy’s new terms, set to take effect on Dec. 16, says the company and its ‘third party partners and vendors’ reserve the right to use sellers’ content to ‘develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies.'” Etsy is already backing down, as it should in my opinion.

item.title: Disney and AWS Team Up to Create AI-Powered ‘Star Wars’ Robots
item.description: Hollywood Reporter: “The audio-animatronic robots in question are The Anzellans: Vilo Vele, Kado Bre’a and Jibu Bre’a, an alien species from the Star Wars galaxy that featured in the 2026 film The Mandalorian and Grogu that will make their public debut at Amazon re:Invent in Las vegas later this month. They were designed by Disney’s Imagineers, though they are powered by AWS.”

item.title: Influencer deepfakes used to stoke Canada-US tensions
item.description: AFP: “Jasmin Laine has hundreds of thousands of subscribers, but some videos of her discussing the Canada-US trade war contain words she says she never spoke. Laine is one of hundreds of content creators who, according to researchers at McGill University, had their identities stolen by a network using artificial intelligence to inflame the online conversation around the crumbling ties between the North American neighbors.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: Open Metropolitan
item.description: I found this in my RSS feeds. I inferred from poking around that it’s been around over a year but has received significant upgrades in the last few months: From the About popup: “Explore more than 340,000 artworks from The Met…. Drag the gallery until something catches your eye. Select any artwork to discover more like it. Use Search and Time Machine to jump across ideas and eras.” Searching for “strawberry” found a gratifying variety of results. Search was a little slow.

item.title: Snowchive
item.description: Found in my RSS feeds: From the About page: “This is a searchable archive of all published documents from the 2013 Snowden disclosures. The archive includes documents published alongside news reporting, The Intercept’s bulk SIDtoday release, and FOIA material (official releases from FOIA litigation and FISC and ODNI declassifications). Every document carries its original PDF, page images, extracted text, and curated metadata – agencies, programs, countries, classification markings, people, and the journalists and articles that published it.”

item.title: Google Employees Petition to Let Schools Use Search Without AI
item.description: Gizmodo: “More than 500 Google workers have signed a petition asking company leadership to allow schools to access Google Search without having to deal with the company’s AI features.”

item.title: Archive of Our Own And Fanlore Are Down For Preventative Maintenance
item.description: Bleeding Cool: “Archive of Our Own and Fanlore have both gone down for ‘preventative maintenance,’ and it’s fine; there is nothing to worry about, we knew this could (and likely would) happen.”

item.title: YouTube will start boosting public view counts when you watch on a TV
item.description: Engadget: “How, you might wonder, will YouTube know who else is watching besides the account-holder? The platform emphasized that it won’t use “devices, cameras, microphones or anything like that.” Rather, views will be estimated using a ‘privacy-safe statistical mode’ based on things like demographic patterns and viewing times, calibrated against real-life testing data. YouTube didn’t share any other methodology details.”

item.title: In the land that gave us ‘cinema,’ activist archivists are bringing back old home movies
item.description: Associated Press: “For Stephanie Ange, Pierre Bouchut and Margot Lestien, who roam from town to town in France, collecting home movies and digitizing them for archives, image preservation is a battle waged reel by reel. The name that the trio chose for their group, Ofnibus, plays off the French word for UFO. They can never be sure what they might find on the films and video cassettes that people bring them, often without much of a clue of what they show.”

item.title: Bloomscrolling: the uplifting new way to waste your own time
item.description: The Guardian: “In fact, bloomscrolling is the precise opposite of doomscrolling. Doomscrolling is where you sit for hours, wasting your life, thumbing through an infinite loop of algorithmically derived depressing posts. Whereas bloomscrolling … Is where you sit for hours, wasting your life, thumbing through an infinite loop of algorithmically derived nice posts.”

item.title: Google says it stops 99% of bad ads. Experts find deceptive ads still appear to users millions of times.
item.description: DigitalTrends: “A study from NYU Tandon and Radboud University has found that tens of thousands of deceptive software ads slipped through Google’s filters and were displayed over 100 million times in Europe. The researchers developed an AI tool called AdLens, which they used to analyze 188,834 software-related ads that had been gathered in March 2026 from Google’s Ads Transparency Center.”

item.title: Oldest church archives in US will move to new location in 2027
item.description: Christian Post: “The Archives of The Episcopal Church, reportedly the oldest denominational archives in the United States, will move to a permanent location in Georgia next year….Created by The Episcopal Church General Convention in 1835, the archives boast thousands of artifacts and documents related to the denomination’s history, with an online catalog of more than 200 sections.”

item.title: We’re Publishing the Tariff Refunds the Government Has Refused to Disclose
item.description: ProPublica: “Today, ProPublica published ‘Cash Back,’ a database of figures on refunds for tariffs paid under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. The database includes 343 public companies for which we found mentions of refunds, amounting to more than $28 billion recovered or expected.”

item.title: PastClimate
item.description: Came in over the transom: “Destination guides for 862 places, ranked by the month you’re travelling and backed by 10–20 years of hourly climate records across 29 countries — with the holiday calendars, moon and sky events, and time tools to plan around them.” Free tier is limited but more than sufficient to explore.

item.title: Free, fast geolocation search at geo.chofter.com
item.description: Shane O’Sullivan: “I found myself repeatedly building apps that needed the geolocation of a place and being frustrated with the available offerings. The GeoNames.org service is great, but their free tier is fairly limited, and if an app becomes successful it can become expensive to use. Other services have more restrictive free tiers and more expensive paid tiers.” Note this is for city/town level geolocation, not address level.

item.title: Meta removes accounts flagged for election meddling
item.description: Reuters: “Taiwan has flagged nearly 2,700 social media accounts to Meta that it says appear to be part of a Chinese information warfare campaign seeking to influence ​elections on Saturday next week, three government officials and internal reports said. In recent weeks, Taiwanese officials identified the accounts on Threads as suspected vehicles for coordinated Chinese influence operations, according to the officials familiar with the matter and the government reports reviewed by Reuters.”

item.title: Archives go quiet
item.description: Daily Tribune (Philippines): “I often go back to government websites when I need to check something I remember reading years ago — a presidential statement, a government program, even an old news report. It’s not exciting, but useful. You search for the story, check the date, make sure it matches what you remember, and move on. Lately, though, people have been doing the same thing with the Philippine News Agency (PNA) website — and ending up empty-handed.”

item.title: We the Vloggers
item.description: Slate: “He clips his phone into a tripod, dons a black tactical vest with a GoPro 360 attached to one shoulder, and affixes a wireless microphone to his cornflower blue T-shirt. If this doesn’t sound like the usual gear an auditor might carry, that’s because [Jeremy] Bartlett isn’t an accountant visiting the housing authority to open the books and make sure the numbers add up. He’s a ‘First Amendment auditor,’ one of an extremely online group of people who see their mission as holding the government accountable and defending the public’s right to take photos and videos in public spaces by doing just that—sometimes with combustible results.”

item.title: A cyberattack using artificial intelligence targeted the EU in October, official says
item.description: Associated Press: “Cybersecurity experts have been dealing with an AI-generated attack on a key European Union institution for almost a month, an official confirmed on Thursday, with some of the bloc’s digital tools still offline. The official did not elaborate on the cyberattack, or say who could have been behind it. It was the first time the 27-member bloc reported a cyberattack using an AI tool.”

item.title: ‘Looksmaxxing’ influencer Clavicular indicted on Cape Cod rape charges
item.description: NBC Boston: “The social media influencer known as Clavicular has been indicted on two rape charges. Braden Peters already pleaded not guilty to a rape charge last month and was released on 10,000 bail. The indictment moves the case to Barnstable Superior Court.”

item.title: New research project to analyse royal documents at the dawn of medieval Europe
item.description: University of Exeter: “Historians will examine and transcribe royal documents issued by Conrad I (911-918) and Henry I (919-36) to develop a greater understanding of life in the early years of the emerging German kingdom…. The project team at the University of Exeter and Monumenta Germaniae Historica in Munich will visit 22 archives across Europe and Britain to study their collections of charters and create an open-access digital edition and research tool.”

item.title: Hunter Professor Examines How Social Media Amplifies Voices Behind Bars
item.description: Hunter College: “…as social media transformed how Americans document their lives, [Professor Calvin John] Smiley noticed something new: Incarcerated and formerly incarcerated people were using platforms such as Instagram and TikTok to tell their own stories, build communities, advocate for change, and shape public understanding of life behind bars. Those observations became the foundation for Prison Hashtags: Incarceration, Reentry, and Digital Identity, his new book with co-author Jan Haldipur, which the two discussed on November 5 at Roosevelt House in a conversation with Columbia University social-work professor Rob Eschmann.”

item.title: Quantum Physics Can Verify a Person’s Location, NIST Researchers Show
item.description: NIST: “In a first-of-its-kind experiment, scientists at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and their colleagues have demonstrated that the quirks of quantum mechanics can definitively confirm the location of a person. Using exquisitely sensitive quantum sensors and quantum technologies developed at NIST, physicist Krister Shalm and an international team of collaborators eliminated loopholes that had left other quantum-based verification strategies vulnerable to fraudsters.”

item.title: (2026) Project Sunset
item.description: A Blue Star: “My apartment window in Burnaby faces due west, toward downtown Vancouver. The sun sets somewhere in that view every evening, but where it sets moves a long way over the year. In December it goes down left of the city. In June it sets far off to the right, behind the mountains. Project Sunset is a camera at that window for five years. It takes a photo every five minutes, day and night, and keeps every one. The sunset is the subject. The real run starts on the winter solstice, December 21, 2026. The pilot is running now.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: ChatGPT Helped “Sadistic” School Shooter Build 3D-Printed Weapons
item.description: Mother Jones: “In September 2025, Jesse Van Rootselaar asked ChatGPT for some advice. The troubled teenager living in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, was planning to test “if my magazine cycles in my gun” and wanted to know if it was necessary to use dummy rounds instead of real ammunition. ‘You can load a magazine with live rounds and cycle the action to check whether the magazine feeds a round into the chamber,’ OpenAI’s chatbot replied, explaining mechanics and safety risks.”

item.title: AI models can be tricked into identifying civilians as military targets by telling them it’s a game
item.description: TechCrunch: “Some AI models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and other leading AI labs could be easily tricked into identifying targets for military strikes — even if they include civilians or locations like schools — simply by being told they’re playing a game, according to a new research report by Vals.”

item.title: Ohio approves two large power plants exclusively for data centers
item.description: Signal Akron: “State officials on Thursday approved permits for two natural gas-fired power plants, large enough to fuel entire cities, for the private use of two data center campuses in Central Ohio.”

item.title: San Francisco Extends Its Data Center Ban, and Two of the City’s Three Stand-Alone Centers Are in the Bayview
item.description: The Sun-Reporter: “The city’s power grid is close to full. Two of San Francisco’s three stand-alone data centers sit in the Bayview. And nobody will be approved to build a new one anywhere in the city for most of the coming year. The Board of Supervisors voted unanimously Tuesday to extend San Francisco’s ban on new data centers by 10 months and 15 days past the 45-day freeze that took effect in October.”

item.title: Canva Now Lets Users Turn Off Generative AI Features
item.description: PetaPixel: “Canva has introduced new settings that allow users to disable its generative AI features and reduce the amount of AI-generated material shown in its content library.”

item.title: Advocates rally for data center reforms
item.description: Evanston Now: “The residents came via bus, car and Amtrak from around the state to call for passage of the POWER Act, a bill that would require data centers to pay to create the energy they consume, mandate transparency around water use, limit noise levels and diesel generator use, ensure local community benefit agreements, and more. The bill failed to progress during the spring legislative session, but advocates hope to see it passed during the veto session.”

item.title: Uncensored AI models are thriving on code hosting platforms
item.description: The Register: “Uncensored large language models (ULLMs) capable of producing harmful content are readily available at popular model-hosting websites, calling into question AI industry commitments to safety.”

item.title: Nigeria drives African push to tackle AI-generated misinformation
item.description: Technology Times (Nigeria): “Nigeria is seeking a coordinated African response to artificial intelligence (AI)-generated misinformation, with the country’s Minister of Information proposing renewed cooperation among governments to combat manipulated digital content and strengthen public trust.”

item.title: Your Google AI mode searches can stay private now with ‘temporary threads’ – here’s how
item.description: ZDNet: “Most of the major AIs offer a temporary chat or incognito option in which your conversation remains private and vanishes as soon as your chat ends. Now Google has jumped on board this bandwagon with its AI Mode searches.”

item.title: Microsoft Confirms Ads Are In AI Overviews On Bing Search
item.description: Search Engine Roundtable: “Microsoft has just confirmed that it is now shows ads in AI Overviews in Bing Search. We started seeing ads in Bing AI Overviews about three weeks ago, and Microsoft has now confirmed this on the Microsoft Advertising blog.”

item.title: Traumatized teens sue school, cops after Doritos bag triggers AI gun alert
item.description: Ars Technica: “The cops did not just target the suspected gunman but apparently told the other teens that they were guilty ‘by association’ when they asked why they were searched. Suing to stop any other teens from facing allegedly life-or-death situations due to officials’ blind trust of AI, the teens have asked for an injunction barring [Baltimore County Public Schools] from using Omnilert until they can effectively establish protocols to prevent police responses to false alerts.”

item.title: Court Tells Cops That The 4th Amendment Doesn’t Cover AI-Generated ‘Probable Cause’
item.description: Techdirt: “AI is pretty much everywhere, and if a court says an algorithm can’t make probable cause determinations, it affects/infects everything from facial recognition tech to predictive policing software to Axon adding AI shovelware to its omnipresent body cameras under the (correct) assumption cops don’t like writing reports. In this case, Alain Osorio was arrested for allegedly passing a bad check at local bank. The only pictures of the suspect came from the bank’s CCTV footage. This was handed over to Detective Ryan Kilmer of the Florence (KY) Police Department.”

item.title: New Study Reveals AI Guardrails Are Easy to Break
item.description: Georgia State University: “The companies that build artificial intelligence invest heavily in guardrails that train AI to refuse harmful requests. New research, recently accepted for publication at the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence Conference on Web and Social Media, suggests those guardrails are far easier to break than many people assume. In tests, a small amount of tampering turned popular AI agents into persistent online harassers.”

item.title: UH researchers use AI to prevent crop damage by predicting spread of invasive beetles
item.description: Big Island Now: “Researchers at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa are developing an artificial intelligence tool to protect agricultural lands by predicting where the invasive coconut rhinoceros beetle is most likely to spread. The $300,000 project will help field crews decide where to place pheromone-baited traps and look for new infestations on Hawaiʻi Island, Kauaʻi and Maui.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: The MIT Processor Database brings decades of chip history into the AI era
item.description: MIT: “Led by MIT FutureTech Project Director Neil Thompson, this project is an effort to create the most comprehensive source of information for hardware chips. The database will offer a foundational tool for industry leaders weighing critical hardware decisions in the age of AI, engineers building new chips, and researchers studying trend lines in economics, computing, AI adoption, and more.”

item.title: NMU Launches UP Regional Data & Intelligence Hub
item.description: Northern Michigan University: “A newly launched U.P. Regional Data & Intelligence Hub makes public economic data from every county in the Upper Peninsula easily accessible, with automatic weekly updates and a simple, interactive online dashboard…. The database is accessible via NMU’s Center for Economic Education and Entrepreneurship website and showcases a number of economic indicators by county, such as employment and salary trends, housing median value trends and workforce composition.”

item.title: 9 Million Images
item.description: Unsplash Blog: “When celebrating 9 million images, the community celebrates 9 million global perspectives. Just by scrolling the Unsplash home feed, the Unsplash community reflects hundreds of countries from around the world. With a global community of over close to 500,000 contributors, we are seeing the world through so many different points of view.”

item.title: WordPress 7.1.5 Release
item.description: WordPress: “This security release features fixes for multiple issues. Because this is a security release, it is recommended that you update your sites immediately.”

item.title: Europe is replacing the big US apps in its offices, and you can use most of the replacements
item.description: MakeUseOf: “On June 4, 2026, the European Parliament switched the default search engine on its work browsers from Google to Qwant. France is also getting ready to move government employees off Zoom and Microsoft Teams. Across Europe, more and more officials are becoming less comfortable relying on just a few big U.S. tech companies to power their public offices. What really stood out to me is that anyone with a web browser or a Windows PC can use many of these same replacements. You can test out quite a few for free, even though some come with a bit of red tape.”

item.title: A cyberattack leaks thousands of Chase customer emails and some phone numbers
item.description: Associated Press: “Personal information belonging to thousands of JPMorgan Chase customers was leaked onto the internet Thursday after third-party vendors at the bank were targeted in a cyberattack. The leak is unrelated a bank outage earlier this week and the information involved did not include credit card or particularly sensitive personal information, the bank said.”

item.title: California Department of Education, private testing company sued over student data hack
item.description: EdSource: “A former public school student is suing the California Department of Education after a major data breach revealed last month exposed demographic information, residential addresses and disability records of millions of California students, reported The Sacramento Bee.”

item.title: Surveillance Isn’t Safety: A Comic About Organizing Against Flock and Other Foes
item.description: EFF: “In the new comic ‘Surveillance Isn’t Safety’—available for free today— cartoonist Bryn Adams explores the growing movement against mass surveillance through their involvement in the community fight against Flock Safety in Cleveland, Ohio. It’s a personal journey that will resonate widely with residents in hundreds of cities where communities are drawing the line against automated license plate readers (ALPRs).”

item.title: Scotland’s museums highlight financial and workforce pressures
item.description: Museums Association: “Just under a fifth of Scotland’s museums (17%) believe a venue they operate could be at risk of closure within the next 12 months, according to a new survey by Museums Galleries Scotland (MGS) – up from 11% two years ago. The 2026 Survey of Scotland’s Museums and Galleries was commissioned by MGS and conducted by DC Research to give an overview of the sector’s activity, contribution and operating conditions. It follows two previous surveys in 2024 and 2022.”

item.title: Why I’m Turning Off Comments on My Blog
item.description: Lireo Designs: “Since the beginning of 2026, I’ve been averaging 300 spam comments each month on my blog posts. And I publish less than 10 posts a month.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Three decades of British East and South East Asian theatre documented and celebrated
item.description: University of Exeter: “A project team, co-led by the University of Exeter and the Royal Central School of Speech and Drama (RCSSD), have collated and documented more than 15,000 items following an extensive process, and these are now safely housed at the V&A East Storehouse. The team has also launched a digital version of the archive, which also includes 30 oral history interviews with artists, producers and theatre makers of several generations who were part of the New Earth Theatre’s story.”

item.title: The CIA’s Covert Playbook in Cuba: An “AMTRUNK” Precedent
item.description: National Security Archives: “In a Top Secret proposal to the CIA director, a high-ranking Directorate of Operations official recommended a ‘pincers strategy’ to bring down the Cuban government, according to declassified operational records published today by the National Security Archive. The March 1963 proposal called for combining ‘economic strangulation to weaken and undermine the regime…with an intensive probing effort to identify and establish channels of communication to disaffected and potentially dissident non-Communist elements in the power centers of the regime.'”

item.title: GTA 6 is already breaking Twitch records
item.description: Polygon: “Grand Theft Auto 6 is already rewriting streaming history. Rockstar Games’ highly anticipated sequel has attracted 3.29 million concurrent viewers on Twitch, breaking the platform’s previous record for a video game launch as its global rollout continues.”

item.title: Google Play unveils the best apps, games, and books of 2026
item.description: Google Blog: “Today, we’re sharing the winners of our annual Best of Play awards — and celebrating the incredible creativity, passion, and technical polish that developers bring to our screens. Google Play is defined by the achievements of the developers and publishers who build for it. These awards are designed to put their outstanding work front and center, both on and off the store.”

item.title: I pulled my internet for 48 hours. Here’s what Project NOMAD could (and couldn’t) replace
item.description: MakeUseOf: “I had been hosting Project NOMAD on my server for months, and I wondered whether an offline knowledge server could really replace the internet if my connection suddenly went down…. Project NOMAD is essentially a self-hosted offline knowledge server. It puts curated references, wikis, maps, courses, and optional local AI behind a browser dashboard you can access from your own network. That sounds useful in theory, but I wanted to know how it held up when the internet was actually gone.”

item.title: Social Media Post Yields New Collection and New Stories
item.description: Maine State Museum: “In April 2026, the Maine State Museum shared an ambrotype photograph of thirteen-year-old Civil War drummer boy Daniel ‘Dannie’ Marston of Phillips, Maine, on its social media platforms. The post caught the attention of family descendant Robert Marston of Presque Isle, who reached out to the Museum with a remarkable family connection.”

item.title: Hank Green is self-funding ClockwiseTV, a curated educational video platform for kids
item.description: TechCrunch: “At the start of each viewing session, the parent and child decide how long they can watch, and the platform will recommend videos that will adhere to that time frame. If a kid is in the midst of a 30-minute session and has already watched two 10-minute videos, they’re not going to be suggested a 20-minute video when they only have 10 minutes left. The startup is addressing a pretty widespread concern among parents, who are worried about more than simply negotiating with their children about how long they can use the iPad.”

item.title: International Press Institute Donates Its Digital Reports to the Archivum
item.description: The Blinken OSA Archivum: “The International Press Institute (IPI), a global organization founded in 1950 at Columbia University dedicated to the promotion and protection of press freedom and the improvement of journalism practices, donated its digital collection of IPI Report to the Blinken OSA Archivum.”

item.title: Report: National Cyber Director To Resign
item.description: iHeartRadio: “The White House’s National Cyber Director, Sean Cairncross, is reportedly stepping down from his position. Axios reports that Cairncross is leaving to allow the White House time to secure Senate confirmation of a new director before Democrats take control of Congress in January.”

item.title: UK Culture Minister Delivers Emotional Plea To YouTube To “Set An Example” & Remove Russell Brand’s Channel
item.description: Deadline: “The UK government minister responsible for film and TV has made a personal plea to YouTube to ‘set an example’ and remove Russell Brand’s channel. Earlier, and under pressure, the Google-owned behemoth said it was investigating the video in which Brand’s wife Laura protested his innocence via a statement he sent her from prison.”

item.title: Website owners thumb their noses at EU privacy rules, researcher finds
item.description: The Register: “Privacy? What privacy? The 100 most-visited English-language sites are flouting European data protection laws on a massive scale, according to a privacy researcher’s investigation.”

item.title: Using New Tools to Help Save the Past for the Future
item.description: University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee: “Xiangming (Simon) Mu, associate professor of information studies, and Quanyi (Monica) Zhao, an MFA candidate in the Peck School of the Arts and associate professor at Hubei University of Technology (China), recently presented their proposal for a digital heritage project to an international audience. Their ‘Living Heritage Ledger’ was one of only six out of more than 600 submissions from 90 countries selected as winners of the United Nations’ Beyonds Challenge. It was featured at the Beyonds Festival-2026 in Geneva in early October.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Muse privacy invasions are freaking out Meta staffers, internal chats show
item.description: Ars Technica: “After some early adopters of Meta’s Muse AI agent complained that it was spying on private messages and behaving unpredictably earlier this fall, Reuters exposed internal chats showing that Meta staff had raised the same alarms.”

item.title: Paris Hilton pushes for law against deepfakes: ‘I want to help build a world that’s safe’
item.description: PBS: “The growing use of artificial intelligence to create sexually explicit images of people without their consent is raising new concerns about privacy, exploitation and the laws meant to protect victims. Among those calling for greater protections is Paris Hilton. She was on Capitol Hill this week urging lawmakers to pass the bipartisan DEFIANCE Act.”

item.title: Navajo Nation Council to weigh data center in San Juan County
item.description: Santa Fe New Mexican: “The Navajo Tribal Utility Authority is pushing to build a data center in San Juan County as part of a sprawling energy and manufacturing campus — a proposal that could go before the full Navajo Nation Council for a vote as soon as next month.”

item.title: Black Neighborhoods Are Twice as Likely To House a Data Center, Study Finds
item.description: 404 Media: “Developers build data centers in communities of color at more than twice the rate they do in white neighborhoods, according to a new study from researchers at George Washington University and the Center for Security, Innovation & New Technology (CSINT) at American University.”

item.title: After gutting newsrooms, McClatchy plans to rebuild itself around AI
item.description: NiemanLab: “Two months after McClatchy Media laid off more than 90 journalists nationwide, executives at the storied local newspaper chain offered a blunt assessment of its future. The award-winning local journalism that has long powered the 169-year-old company was no longer a viable business model, executives told McClatchy employees during a virtual town hall this month, and its survival depended on a wholesale reinvention — centered entirely around artificial intelligence.”

item.title: Nearly 80% of ACE Editors Surveyed Are Using AI, New Report Finds: ‘You Adapt or Die’
item.description: Variety: “There are many whispers in Hollywood about how many professionals are secretly using AI tools. Now a cohort of film editors is ready to go public. In a survey of 120 members of the 1,200-body American Cinema Editors conducted by Avid, the tech company behind editing software stalwarts like Media Composer and Pro Tools, 77.5% of film editors are using AI to some extent in the post-production process.”

item.title: US Catholic bishops’ new AI task force urges regulation and worker protections
item.description: Associated Press: “Bishop Oscar Cantú of San Jose, California, emphasized the unique role the U.S. church is well-positioned to play when he addressed his colleagues at the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops’ annual fall gathering Wednesday. From his Silicon Valley diocese, Cantú chairs the conference’s new AI task force focused on preserving human dignity.”

item.title: ‘They should be subsidizing the ratepayers’: NC governor says data center subsidies should be rolled back
item.description: Politico: “North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein said his state needs to roll back subsidies for data centers, telling POLITICO that Big Tech companies should be ‘paying their own way.'”

item.title: Culture ministry launches new AI search engine. Next target: AI-led tracking of stolen antiquities
item.description: The Print (India): “The Union Ministry of Culture Monday launched an AI-based search engine and a chatbot named ‘Sanskriti’ on its main website, with both drawing answers only from the roughly 65 portals run by the ministry and its institutions.”

item.title: The Anti-A.I. Campus Movement Is Growing
item.description: New York Times: “Last March, a handful of students at Transylvania University created a petition, attempting to slow the advance of artificial intelligence on their campus. It asked the administration to cancel chatbot licenses with A.I. giants and instead invest the money in ‘human-centered education.’ About a third of the college’s students signed on.”

item.title: Young People Hate AI CEOs So Passionately That It’s Almost Hard to Believe
item.description: Futurism: “Asked ‘who do you trust to act responsibly on AI?’ the vast majority of participants said they ‘don’t trust’ any of the nine figures. Palantir’s extremely controversial CEO Alex Karp scored the lowest, with 81 percent choosing ‘don’t trust,’ while Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella fared the best — albeit with a pitiful 35 percent ‘trust’ score. Everyone else fell in between: 79 percent of respondents said they don’t trust Peter Thiel, while a whopping 71, 70, and 69 percent said they ‘don’t trust’ Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk, and Sam Altman, respectively (Musk will probably be mad he didn’t get that 69 figure.)”

item.title: Snapchat now lets developers build AR Lenses with AI assistants like Claude Code and Cursor
item.description: TechCrunch: “Snapchat announced on Wednesday that it’s giving Lens creators the ability to build Lenses using the AI coding assistants they already use, like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex. Snapchat Lenses, which are a core part of the social network’s platform, are AR effects that let users alter their appearance, add digital objects to their surroundings, or interact with animated experiences through the camera.”

item.title: A Kentucky man becomes the first humanist granted religious exemption from AI
item.description: Religion News Service: “David Durman, an administrator at the University of Kentucky, said using AI would cause him to offload his thinking and decision making, which would violate his humanist views. He hopes other Americans will rethink their views on AI, too.”

item.title: Arizona Says It Is Investigating OpenAI, Other Firms Over Possible Rogue Agents
item.description: Reuters: “The state ⁠of ⁠Arizona has opened a ⁠criminal investigation into OpenAI and other AI companies relating ​to the ‘apparent infiltration of banks by rogue AI agents,’ Arizona Attorney General Kris ‌Mayes said Wednesday.”

item.title: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths
item.description: The Guardian: “Since 2017, the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand the contents of 16 notebooks that Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. This material – the ‘workbooks’ – is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic. Much of it is written in a German shorthand, Gabelsberger, that was obsolete even when Gödel was using it. Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow – about a page a week – until September, when von Plato enlisted the help of the AI model Claude.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: U.S. School Districts Weigh Breaking Up With Google Search Over A.I.
item.description: New York Times: “Starting next year, Google said, its A.I.-related products, including Search and its Gemini app, will be turned off automatically for schools, and administrators can choose to turn those A.I. tools on. But there will be no version of search available without A.I. chatbot features, meaning schools that want to forgo A.I. will lose access to an important learning tool.” [As the co-author of GOOGLE HACKS, my official comment is UGGGGHHHHHHHHHH – TJC]

item.title: I refused to pay a subscription just to track my subscriptions, so I self-hosted this open-source dashboard
item.description: MakeUseOf: “Wallos is a free, open-source subscription tracker that you can self-host to manage your existing and upcoming recurring payments. The developer presents it as a better alternative to complicated Excel sheets or paid financial management software. This benefit is in addition to the fact that your spending information never touches anyone else’s servers.”

item.title: Project Gryffindor: Meta’s plan to get more school kids using Instagram
item.description: NPR: “Internal Meta documents show the company planned to boost Instagram use among teens by targeting schools in an initiative it named ‘Project Gryffindor.’ The project focused on growing what it called ‘school communities’ in the U.S. by encouraging teens to include their school banner on their profiles and establishing a student directory that allows users to see and connect with others from their school who use the platform.”

item.title: Google commemorates Robert Pattinson’s James Bond casting with a sneaky Easter egg
item.description: Mashable: “Robert Pattinson’s casting as James Bond has left Google feeling shaken, not stirred. Following the announcement that Pattinson would be our next 007, Google introduced a new Bond-themed Easter egg.”

item.title: A Canadian teen was blackmailed after sending nude images. AP/FRONTLINE found his scammer in Nigeria
item.description: Associated Press: “The teen was trapped in a scam that increasingly targets young men: Sextortion. The FBI has warned of a surge in financially motivated sextortion of minors – threatening to expose people’s private images unless they send money. This year is on track to be the worst ever. By August, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) had received more than 40,000 reports of financial sextortion, against a total of 50,000 for all of last year. The impact can be lethal: Dozens of young people have taken their own lives after being sextorted.”

item.title: New York Sued Over Law Requiring Social Media Platforms to Display Warning Labels
item.description: PetaPixel: “New York has been sued by an internet trade group, which includes YouTube, Facebook and Instagram, over its plans to require social media platforms to put warning labels for users. New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed the warning label law in November last year. The legislation — which is scheduled to take effect on January 1, 2027. — will require social media platforms that offer addictive features, such as algorithmic feeds, autoplay, infinite scrolling, like counts and push notifications, to display warning labels.”

item.title: British Scattered Spider hacker sentenced to 6 years in prison
item.description: Bleeping Computer: “A leader of the Scattered Spider cybercrime collective has been sentenced to six years in prison in the United States for stealing millions in cryptocurrency and conspiring to hack a dozen companies. US prosecutors charged 24-year-old British man Tyler Robert Buchanan and four other suspects in November with wire fraud and aggravated identity theft in relation to a series of phishing attacks between September 2021 and April 2023.”

item.title: Among social media ads, short-form video drives the most actions
item.description: Tubefilter: “Social media advertising continues to grow, but not all ads are created equal. The ad tech company DoubleVerify has released its 2026 Global Insights Report, a dispatch that identifies YouTube and Facebook — and their respective short-form formats — as dominant forces in the social media marketing landscape.”

item.title: DJI Names Winners of Its 3D Heritage Contest
item.description: Radiance Fields: “DJI has named the winners of its World Heritage 3D Conservation Initiative, a contest for flythrough videos of heritage sites reconstructed from DJI drone data. Every entry had to be an MP4 rendered in DJI Reality, the free viewer DJI added to Terra 5.2.0 in March, from a 3D model of a heritage site, and DJI’s contest page says Reality generates those flythroughs from mesh, 3D Gaussian splatting or point cloud data.”

item.title: Pakistan’s solar revolution is so successful the national grid is lagging behind
item.description: BBC: “Pakistan has seen a boom in imported solar panels, which glisten from the rooftops of homes and hospitals; from farmers’ fields to industrial complexes. From 2018 to 2025, the share of electricity generated from solar energy in the country rose from 1% to 28%, according to Pakistan-based think tank Renewables First, with some seven million households now owning panels.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: FPPC Launches New Features to Expand Public Access to Officials’ Financial Disclosures
item.description: Fair Political Practices Commission: “The California Fair Political Practices Commission (FPPC) today announced the launch of new searches and export tools of its Public Official Financial Disclosure Portal, expanding the public’s ability to search, review, and download financial disclosure information filed by public officials. The latest update introduces several new features, including the ability to export search results and filings, conduct targeted searches for gifts and travel payments, and search across multiple filing years simultaneously.”

item.title: War of 1812 Pension Files: Fully Digitized and Available with Full-Text Search!
item.description: Fold3 Blog: “We have incredible news! A monumental 16-year preservation initiative has crossed the finish line! All 90,000 War of 1812 Pension Files are now completely digitized and freely accessible to the public. Even better, Fold3 has enabled full-text search across the entire collection, powered by our patent-pending Transcription Viewer.”

item.title: Thundermail Q4 2026 recap: new features, your feedback, and what’s next
item.description: Thunderbird Blog: “It has been quite a year. When we started welcoming our first Early Birds into Thundermail, we had a waitlist, a vision, and a lot of work ahead of us. Since then, thousands of you have joined, tested, filed ideas, and helped us shape what this service is becoming. The upcoming new year is a great chance to look back at everything we’ve built together and what we have coming up in 2027.”

item.title: Elon Musk says: ‘I’m not MAGA’
item.description: TechCrunch: “Elon Musk, who spent $277 million to get Donald Trump re-elected president in 2024 and who, during that campaign, declared himself ‘dark MAGA’ and who, after the election, was subsequently photographed sporting a cartoonishly large MAGA hat while visiting the Oval Office, has some news for Americans: none of that necessarily makes him MAGA.”

item.title: TikTok creators are joining Disney+ as Hulu integration wraps up
item.description: Mashable: “Disney shared the timing in its fiscal fourth-quarter earnings announcement on Nov. 17, saying the rollout will coincide with the buildup to Marvel’s Avengers: Doomsday, which opens in theaters Dec. 18. The launch gives a date to the content-sharing partnership Disney and TikTok first announced in August, which lets participating creators make short videos using material from Disney’s movies and series. It’s also another sign of how closely streaming services are watching the creator economy.”

item.title: Anti-vaccine group once led by RFK Jr back on Facebook and Instagram after being banned
item.description: The Guardian: “An anti-vaccine group led for years by Robert F Kennedy Jr has been allowed back on Facebook and Instagram, four years after Meta removed the group for repeatedly violating its misinformation policies.”

item.title: History Colorado is the first to claim sports betting caused it to lose money
item.description: Denver Post: “History Colorado is the first organization to blame online sports betting for lost revenue in the more than six years that sports gambling has been legal in the state. Now one of the state’s premier cultural institutions is asking gambling regulators to tap a fund set aside for local governments and organizations that can show legalized sports betting has hurt their bottom line.”

item.title: Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
item.description: Krebs on Security: “Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds. Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.”

item.title: EU sanctions Kremlin troll factory, hacker group in new push against Russian hybrid activities
item.description: Kyiv Independent: “The EU on Nov. 16 adopted new sanctions against two entities and 30 individuals involved in Russia’s disinformation and cyberwarfare activities, including the Kremlin-backed Social Design Agency (SDA). The Council of the EU adopted the package as Western officials raise alarm over the growing threat of Russian election interference and other hybrid activities across Europe.”

item.title: Largest British study to check social media ban’s effect on youth mental health
item.description: BBC: “More than 300,000 young people in Britain will work with researchers to help understand how the UK’s forthcoming social media ban for under-16s could affect mental health. The studies will examine the habits of the children and teenagers, including whether they spend less time on their phones and what they are replacing scrolling with.”

item.title: UW’s SER Launches Internal Publication Database
item.description: University of Wyoming: “The University of Wyoming School of Energy Resources (SER) has launched a new centralized database designed to serve as a comprehensive, searchable repository for all SER-affiliated publications. Housed internally, the platform gathers a wide spectrum of research materials, including grant final reports; peer-reviewed articles written by SER faculty and affiliates; white papers, research briefs and community guides; web applications, databases and StoryMaps.”

item.title: Brazil’s approach to deforestation delivers major reductions in Amazon forest loss
item.description: North Carolina State University: “A new study finds that a Brazilian policy aimed at reducing deforestation appears to be remarkably effective and has significantly reduced forest loss in the Brazilian Amazon. The largest reductions occurred on private lands specifically targeted by Brazil’s Priority List (PL) policy, with no evidence that deforestation shifted to other land ownerships or neighboring municipalities.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Study reveals energy demands and emissions of America’s data centers
item.description: PBS News: “The 400 largest data centers in the United States emit more greenhouse gas emissions in one year than the entire nation of Denmark, according to a new report from Harvard University. From May 2024 to April 2025, data centers accounted for nearly 2% of total U.S. energy consumption and produced more than 25 million metric tons of CO2.”

item.title: AI toys are on the naughty list again this year
item.description: The Register: “The Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), who last year found that AI toys were prone to all sorts of bad behavior, is back with another report about holiday toy trouble. They retested last year’s toys as well as three new ones. The results were not very encouraging.”

item.title: Duke Energy push for more NC natural gas plants to power more data centers faces opposition
item.description: Carolina Public Press: “Duke Energy, the electric utility that controls nearly all of North Carolina’s power generation, is pushing forward with a natural gas buildout intended to support a deluge of new data centers. The utility checked off a crucial step in that process Monday evening, when the Davidson County Board of Commissioners approved a rezoning request from Duke to build a liquified natural gas storage facility along the Yadkin River near Lexington.”

item.title: How Much Water Will The Future Maui Data Center Use? The Military Won’t Say
item.description: Honolulu Civil Beat: “The U.S. Air Force and U.S. Space Force have maintained that the 56,000-square-foot laboratory and data center under construction in Kīhei is not expected to be a significant added strain on the region’s infrastructure. But federal officials still won’t say how much water the project is expected to use.”

item.title: Married music teachers are leading Idaho’s AI resistance
item.description: Idaho Education News: “Boise couple Jack and Cathryn Gardner have organized the state’s first AI protest. They’ve been meeting with federal and state lawmakers to push for regulations on the technology, and they’re seeing firsthand how AI influences young students. Cathryn teaches music to elementary students in the Boise School District and Jack, who formerly taught music in the Nampa School District, is a freelance bassist teaching private lessons to high school and college students.”

item.title: Can A.I. Take the Edge Off One of Hollywood’s Worst Jobs?
item.description: New York Times: “Rotoscoping — even the name is insipid — involves methodically tracing around an object or a person, frame by frame and often for hours so that it can be isolated from the rest of the shot. A hologram of Princess Leia does not plead for help from Obi-Wan Kenobi in the original ‘Star Wars’ (1977) without rotoscoping. Nor do the light sabers glow. But can A.I. ease the drudgery? And can it do so with the same expert precision that human hands have provided for decades? What happens to those workers if their jobs get replaced?”

item.title: Texas cities and counties forgo $1 billion in taxes to data centers in exchange for few job guarantees
item.description: Texas Tribune: “Texas cities and counties are giving away more than $1 billion in local property tax revenue to data centers. The Tribune’s analysis found 53 agreements for 34 data centers. The local agreements require minimal job creation. Nearly half had no job stipulations. In total the agreements require 465 jobs.”

item.title: Texas issues air permit for massive SpaceX data center
item.description: Politico, and I will swear to you on the religious volume of your choice that these stories ended up together unintentionally: “Texas environmental regulators issued an air pollution permit Monday to Elon Musk’s SpaceX data center and gas-fired power plant planned for the Rio Grande Valley, saying they have ‘resumed’ permitting of supercomputing facilities after Republican Gov. Greg Abbott ordered the agency to pause approvals in September.”

item.title: ‘Why get a degree?’: How a coding course caused a clash over AI in the U-M School of Information
item.description: Michigan Daily: “A post to Reddit Oct. 24 alleged AI was heavily used in the development of course curriculum for a computer science course in the School of Information, which commenters identified as SI 506 — Programming I. SI 506 is one of just two required core courses for all Master of Science in Information students, which focused in the past on teaching programming fundamentals primarily using Python 3.x script. In the post, a student criticized the course curriculum.”

item.title: Anthropic reportedly prices its IPO at $83 per share, valuing the AI giant at $1.5 trillion
item.description: Associated Press: “Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 per share on Wednesday, according to multiple reports, an amount above the expected price range that values the artificial intelligence giant at $1.5 trillion.”

item.title: Facebook made one quiet change, and increased organic traffic by over 40 million visits a month
item.description: Peripheral: “Search Expert Saul Westbrook researches how Facebook is utilising AI-summarised pages to win organic search, whether it counts as scaled content abuse, and why having strong Facebook presence may be the next new organic strategy that no-one is talking about.”

item.title: China influencer slammed for using AI to ‘resurrect’ grandpa on hit fashion account to grieve
item.description: South China Morning Post: “A Chinese influencer has recreated his grandfather’s videos using artificial intelligence (AI) after the 90-year-old, known for his stylish streetwear modelling, died, sparking online controversy over the ethics of AI resurrection.”

item.title: Google to keep Gemini chats for 2 months, up from 72 hours, even with history off
item.description: TechCrunch: “Google is extending how long it keeps temporary Gemini chats and conversations made with chat history turned off to around two months, saying the change aims to improve safety and security as AI systems become more capable.”

item.title: California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face, other AI model loss of control
item.description: CNBC: “California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Monday sued artificial intelligence giant OpenAI for allegedly endangering the public by developing advanced AI models without adequate safeguards and monitoring.”

item.title: The Part About the Machines
item.description: The Point: “I’ve been following this technology for years, and for a long time I was cynical about it: I told myself that large language models would soon stop improving. Instead, their capabilities have only grown more prodigious. The only thing I believe now is that the years ahead of us are going to be strange and difficult. Our societies will change in response to this technology as much as they changed in response to the printing press, the locomotive, the internet and smartphones. Look at the controversy surrounding this novel; listen to yourselves, listen to us, arguing about the role of the author, of publishers, of the work of art in the age of its mechanical generation. If this past month is any indication, we will only continue to have more debates like this one, debates that will carve out ever-larger sections of our society.” Good evening, Internet…
